German Shepherd.indoor_risk_notes: Can overheat in poorly ventilated indoor spaces. Dense double coat retains heat after outdoor activity.
German Shepherd.outdoor_risk_notes: High surface burn risk on hot pavement. Humidity significantly reduces cooling via panting.
breed_specific_tips: Always check pavement temperature before walks
Use a cooling mat after activity
Morning walks strictly before 8 AM in summer
Brush coat regularly to reduce heat retention

Labrador Retriever.indoor_risk_notes: Generally more heat-tolerant indoors, but overweight tendency can elevate risk significantly.
Labrador Retriever.outdoor_risk_notes: High enthusiasm can mask early heat stress — may continue activity beyond safe limits. Watch paw pads.
breed_specific_tips: Do not rely on the dog to self-regulate activity in heat
Limit fetch sessions to 5 minutes in warm conditions
Ensure constant water access during outdoor time
Monitor for overweight as it significantly increases heat risk

Golden Retriever.indoor_risk_notes: Dense long coat traps heat well after activity. Ensure cool resting surface and airflow.
Golden Retriever.outdoor_risk_notes: Humidity severely impacts cooling for this coat type. Long coat retains ground heat after lying down.
breed_specific_tips: Never skip post-walk cooldown period
Use cooling vest in high-humidity conditions
Avoid midday activity entirely in summer
Provide a cool tile or mat resting zone

Pug.indoor_risk_notes: Even indoor temperatures above 27°C can cause respiratory distress. AC is essential.
Pug.outdoor_risk_notes: Extremely high respiratory risk in humidity. Shortened airway makes cooling nearly impossible at elevated temperatures.
breed_specific_tips: Air conditioning is not optional — it is safety equipment for this breed
Avoid any outdoor exertion above 24°C apparent temperature
Watch breathing rate even at rest during warm weather
Carry portable water and a cooling cloth on all outings

Siberian Husky.indoor_risk_notes: Indoor temperatures above 22°C are already above this breed's comfort zone. Heavy coat retains body heat.
Siberian Husky.outdoor_risk_notes: Primary breed demonstrating human-animal mismatch. Owner may feel comfortable while dog is already stressed.
breed_specific_tips: Even mild human comfort temperatures can be risky for this breed
Never shave the coat — it provides insulation both ways
Provide constant shade and multiple water sources
Avoid any activity when apparent temperature exceeds 25°C

Persian.indoor_risk_notes: Primary risk is indoor heat trap near windows. Long coat + flat face makes cooling very difficult.
Persian.outdoor_risk_notes: Strictly indoor breed. Outdoor exposure even in moderate heat is inadvisable.
breed_specific_tips: Keep sun-facing rooms ventilated during peak hours
Provide ceramic or tile cool zones
Check breathing rate regularly in warm weather
Regular coat grooming reduces heat retention significantly

Maine Coon.indoor_risk_notes: Very large body + heavy coat creates significant indoor heat load. Needs multiple cool zones.
Maine Coon.outdoor_risk_notes: Heavy coat insulates against cold but traps significant heat in warm conditions.
breed_specific_tips: Provide multiple cool resting surfaces across rooms
Ensure fresh water in multiple locations
Light grooming in summer months helps reduce heat retention
Monitor closely when ambient temperature exceeds 26°C

Siamese.indoor_risk_notes: Most heat-tolerant of the supported cat breeds, but dehydration can be subtle and overlooked.
Siamese.outdoor_risk_notes: Relatively adaptable but still at risk from extreme heat. Can be curious and wander into direct sun.
breed_specific_tips: Ensure constant fresh water — dehydration risk can be underestimated
Watch for behavioral changes as heat stress indicator
Even in moderate heat, avoid sun-facing rooms at peak hours
Interactive play should be reduced on hot days

British Shorthair.indoor_risk_notes: Dense plush coat has moderate heat trap effect indoors. Stoic nature may mask discomfort.
British Shorthair.outdoor_risk_notes: Stocky body structure means less surface-area-to-volume ratio, increasing heat retention risk.
breed_specific_tips: Dense coat can mask discomfort — check breathing and behavior
Ensure ventilated sleeping areas during warm nights
Provide fresh cool water multiple times daily
Watch for reduced appetite as early heat stress sign

Sphynx.indoor_risk_notes: Hairless skin absorbs heat from sun patches quickly. Indoor sun traps near windows are a hidden hazard.
Sphynx.outdoor_risk_notes: No coat protection means direct UV exposure risk is high. Not more heat-tolerant despite less fur.
breed_specific_tips: Block direct sun through windows during peak hours
Skin temperature can rise quickly — monitor regularly
Avoid outdoor sun exposure even in moderate temperatures
Ensure cool shaded indoor zones away from windows
